notes: Replaced r5 fork-child-process-id with fork-inherits-working-directory to avoid repeating the new-versus-preserved PID distinction covered by exec-preserves-process-id.

cards.statement: A child created by Linux fork() initially uses the same working directory as its parent.
cards.explanation: fork() gives the child its parent's current working-directory setting, rather than resetting it to a home directory.

cards.statement: A process can get a fresh PID by replacing its program through Linux execve().
cards.explanation: Linux execve() replaces the program running inside an existing process. The process retains its PID across that replacement.
cards.misconception: Replacing a process's program also gives the process a new PID.

cards.statement: On a system booted with systemd, its system service manager runs as PID 1.
cards.explanation: systemd's system instance acts as the init process. Per-user systemd managers are separate instances rather than the system's PID 1.

source.title: systemd(1) — Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: The procps-ng `ps` command can refresh its process listing periodically during a single run.
cards.explanation: procps-ng ps prints a snapshot of selected processes. Its manual directs users to top for a repeatedly updated display.
cards.misconception: ps itself provides a continuously refreshing process monitor.

cards.statement: Linux retains an exited zombie child's termination status for its parent to collect.
cards.explanation: A zombie has finished executing, but Linux keeps its termination information. A parent can collect that information and reap the child with wait().

cards.statement: Linux can resume a job-control-stopped process simply because CPU time becomes available.
cards.explanation: A job-control-stopped process needs a continuation signal to resume execution. Available CPU time alone does not make it runnable again.
cards.misconception: A stopped process is merely waiting for the scheduler to allocate CPU time.

cards.statement: Linux can reparent an orphaned process to a surviving ancestor configured as a child subreaper.
cards.explanation: When a parent exits, Linux selects the nearest living ancestor subreaper if one exists. The orphan then records that subreaper as its new parent.

cards.statement: Raising a Linux process's nice value gives it higher scheduling priority under normal scheduling.
cards.explanation: For normal Linux scheduling, a higher nice value means lower priority. The numeric nice value runs in the opposite direction from scheduling preference.
cards.misconception: A higher numeric nice value means higher scheduling priority.

cards.statement: An unprivileged Linux user can use renice to raise the nice value of a process they own.
cards.explanation: Linux permits an ordinary user to increase an owned process's nice value. This operation does not require administrative privilege.

cards.statement: On Linux, `/proc/PID/cwd` points to the directory that contains the process's executable.
cards.explanation: Linux exposes a process's current working directory through /proc/PID/cwd. That directory can differ from the location of its executable.
cards.misconception: The cwd link describes where the executable is stored rather than where the process is working.

cards.statement: Linux can send SIGTTIN when a background job tries to read from its controlling terminal.
cards.explanation: Terminal input normally belongs to the foreground process group. A background group's read attempt triggers SIGTTIN unless an exception applies.

cards.statement: Linux keeps a terminated process's PID reserved until the next system boot.
cards.explanation: Linux can recycle a PID after the old process is reaped. A stored PID may therefore later refer to an unrelated process.
cards.misconception: Process IDs remain reserved for the entire boot, even after the processes disappear.

cards.statement: `kill PID` sends SIGTERM by default when the caller supplies a positive process ID.
cards.explanation: kill selects SIGTERM as its default signal. Requesting a different signal requires an explicit signal argument.

cards.statement: A Linux process can catch SIGKILL to flush buffered output before it terminates.
cards.explanation: Linux does not allow a process to catch SIGKILL. That signal therefore offers the target no opportunity to run a cleanup handler.
cards.misconception: SIGKILL gives the target a chance to handle the signal and clean up.

cards.statement: With normal settings, the terminal driver sends SIGINT to the foreground process group on Ctrl-C.
cards.explanation: The terminal's interrupt character generates SIGINT for the foreground process group, so a foreground pipeline's processes receive the interrupt together.

cards.statement: With normal settings, the terminal driver uses SIGSTOP to suspend the foreground job on Ctrl-Z.
cards.explanation: The terminal's suspend character, usually Ctrl-Z, generates SIGTSTP. It is distinct from the SIGSTOP signal.
cards.misconception: Ctrl-Z generates SIGSTOP rather than SIGTSTP.

cards.statement: A successful `kill -0 PID` confirms that the target application is responding to requests.
cards.explanation: kill -0 checks that the target exists and that the caller has permission to signal it. It does not test the application's responsiveness.
cards.misconception: A successful zero-signal check is an application health check.

cards.statement: GNU `nohup command` automatically places command in the background of the invoking shell.
cards.explanation: GNU nohup changes hangup handling, not job placement. In a plain nohup command invocation, the shell still waits for the command to finish.
cards.misconception: nohup also launches the command as a background job.

cards.statement: In Bash, `command &` lets the shell continue while command runs as an asynchronous job.
cards.explanation: A trailing & makes Bash launch the command asynchronously. The shell proceeds to its next command rather than waiting for that job to complete.

cards.statement: In Bash, `bg %1` can resume a stopped job while the shell keeps control of the terminal.
cards.explanation: With job control enabled, Bash bg resumes the selected job in the background. The job remains outside the terminal's foreground process group.

cards.statement: In Bash, `disown %1` can terminate job 1 by removing its entry from the shell's job table.
cards.explanation: Bash disown removes a job-table entry rather than terminating the job's processes. Removing shell bookkeeping is not a request to end execution.
cards.misconception: Removing a job with disown also kills its processes.

cards.statement: With huponexit enabled, an interactive Bash login shell sends SIGHUP to its jobs on a normal exit.
cards.explanation: Bash's huponexit option enables sending SIGHUP to jobs when an interactive login shell exits normally. The login-shell condition matters.

cards.statement: An interactive Bash shell with its default signal handling exits when it receives SIGTERM.
cards.explanation: Interactive Bash ignores SIGTERM in the absence of traps. A script or a shell with customized signal handling is a different case.
cards.misconception: An interactive Bash shell follows the usual termination action for SIGTERM by default.

cards.statement: For a command terminated by fatal signal N, Bash reports an exit status of 128+N.
cards.explanation: Bash encodes fatal-signal termination by adding 128 to the signal number. This status describes how the command ended, rather than a normal exit chosen by the program.

cards.statement: In Bash, `command >> log` appends standard output to an existing log file.
cards.explanation: Bash opens the target of >> for appending. Subsequent output goes at the end of the file, preserving the content already there.

cards.statement: In Bash, the `2> errors` redirection selects a command's standard output for the errors file.
cards.explanation: Bash's 2> redirection selects file descriptor 2, which is standard error. In this command, errors receives that stream rather than standard output.
cards.misconception: The 2> redirection selects standard output.

cards.statement: With stdout on a terminal, Bash's `command 2>&1 > log` sends standard error into log.
cards.explanation: Bash applies redirections left to right. Here, 2>&1 first copies stdout's terminal destination; the later > log does not redirect that existing stderr destination.
cards.misconception: Duplicating stdout makes stderr track later changes to stdout's destination.

cards.statement: In Bash, `producer | consumer` passes producer's standard error through the pipe by default.
cards.explanation: A plain Bash pipe connects the producer's standard output to the consumer's standard input. Standard error keeps its separate destination.
cards.misconception: A plain pipe automatically combines standard output and standard error.

cards.statement: With pipefail set, Bash uses the rightmost failure's status for a failed `a | b | c` pipeline.
cards.explanation: Bash's pipefail option selects the rightmost nonzero command status. Rightmost refers to position in the pipeline, not which command finishes last.

cards.statement: With Bash noclobber off, `sort data > data` preserves data's original contents until sorting finishes.
cards.explanation: Bash opens and truncates data for output before starting sort. The input file is therefore already empty when sort begins reading it.
cards.misconception: The shell waits until sorting completes before overwriting the redirected input file.

cards.statement: GNU `tee copy.log` can save its input in a file while sending the same data to standard output.
cards.explanation: GNU tee copies its standard input to the named file and to standard output. That permits saving a stream while passing it onward.

cards.statement: In Bash, `<<'EOF'` lets a here-document contain literal `$HOME` text rather than the variable's value.
cards.explanation: Bash checks whether any part of a here-document's delimiter is quoted. A quoted delimiter suppresses expansions throughout the body.

cards.statement: Bash can pass an empty input stream to cat using the here-string `cat <<< ''`.
cards.explanation: Bash appends a newline to a here-string before supplying it as standard input. Even an empty supplied string therefore produces a newline byte.
cards.misconception: An empty here-string produces zero bytes of input.

cards.statement: In Bash, `value=$(producer)` removes trailing newlines from producer's captured standard output.
cards.explanation: Bash strips trailing newlines from output captured with $(). Newlines within the captured text remain.

cards.statement: In Bash, a builtin `cd` inside `$(...)` can change the outer shell's working directory.
cards.explanation: Bash runs $() commands in a subshell environment. A cd executed there leaves the surrounding shell's working directory unchanged.
cards.misconception: Commands inside $() share the surrounding shell's mutable working-directory state.

cards.statement: In Bash, `command >| log` overrides noclobber protection for an existing regular file.
cards.explanation: Bash's >| operator explicitly bypasses noclobber's protection against replacing an existing regular file. Other restrictions, such as filesystem permissions, still apply.

cards.statement: In Bash, `export REGION=west` puts REGION in the environment of later external commands.
cards.explanation: Bash marks an exported variable for inclusion in child-command environments. The command inherits its value at launch.

cards.statement: In Bash, `source ./settings.sh` can change variables in the current shell.
cards.explanation: Bash source executes a file's commands in the current shell context. Assignments there can therefore remain in that shell after the file finishes.

cards.statement: When Bash searches PATH for an executable, it chooses the last matching directory's executable.
cards.explanation: A Bash PATH search proceeds through directories in their listed order and uses the first suitable executable it finds.
cards.misconception: Later PATH entries take precedence over earlier matching entries during a search.

cards.statement: In Bash, single-quoting `$HOME` as a command argument can expand HOME to its stored value.
cards.explanation: Bash single quotes preserve the enclosed text literally. An argument written as '$HOME' contains those characters, rather than the variable's value.
cards.misconception: Single quotes retain variable expansion while protecting the resulting text.

cards.statement: In Bash, `tool "$@"` can preserve a separate argument for each positional parameter, including empty ones.
cards.explanation: Bash expands "$@" into separate arguments, retaining spaces and empty values within the original parameters. This preserves argument boundaries when forwarding them.

cards.statement: With default IFS in Bash, `items='red blue'; tool $items` passes red and blue as separate arguments.
cards.explanation: Bash applies word splitting to the unquoted expansion of items. The default IFS treats the space between red and blue as a separator.

cards.statement: For matching files, Bash's `ls *.log` lets ls turn the wildcard into filename arguments.
cards.explanation: When *.log matches files, Bash replaces the pattern with their names before invoking ls. ls receives the resulting filename arguments.
cards.misconception: The invoked command performs the shell's filename expansion.

cards.statement: Bash's default `*` expansion includes hidden names such as `.env` in the current directory.
cards.explanation: With Bash's default filename-expansion settings, * skips leading-dot names. Enabling dotglob includes those names in matching.
cards.misconception: The default star pattern includes hidden filenames.

cards.statement: With nullglob and failglob off, Bash passes an unmatched `*.log` pattern as a literal argument.
cards.explanation: Bash leaves a filename pattern unchanged when it has no matches and both nullglob and failglob are disabled. The command receives the pattern text itself.

cards.statement: Bash checks existing filenames to decide which words `{draft,final}.txt` expands into.
cards.explanation: Bash brace expansion generates draft.txt and final.txt textually. The existence of files with those names does not determine the generated words.
cards.misconception: Brace expansion selects names from the filesystem like filename matching does.

cards.statement: Bash returns status 126 when permission checks prevent execution of a command it has found.
cards.explanation: Bash reports a found-but-unexecutable command with status 126. A failed command search instead has status 127 under its normal command handling.

cards.statement: In Bash, `build && deploy` runs deploy when build exits with a failure status.
cards.explanation: Bash runs the command after && when the preceding command returns status zero. A failed build therefore prevents deploy in this list.
cards.misconception: The command after && runs in response to a failure of the preceding command.
